framingNote: These four are starting hypotheses, not answers. They come from a 31-benchmark scan EY has already completed at its own cost, and we set them out so CI can see exactly where we begin and hold us to changing our minds. Activity One exists to test them: the deep-dives will price the shared studio, establish whether a certification mark can fund itself, ask Preferred Hotel Group and SLH what hosting a Keystone collection would actually cost, and put the hard outcome questions to the Boundless Southern Africa and Africa's Eden secretariats. We expect at least one option to be discarded and the recommended model to be a hybrid. Declaring a starting position openly is what makes disagreement possible; a bidder with no starting position has nothing for CI to argue with.

options.name: The Shared Studio
options.archetype: Archetype 1, Shared service (in-house service unit and conservancy association sub-types)
options.oneLine: A central brand studio, toolkit and data spine that the emerging areas draw down on, delivered through the conservancy associations that already serve them, underwritten by CI and Keystone donors at the start and shifting to association subscriptions and per-unit production charges.
options.offer: One modular brand system every area applies to its own content: identity templates, map and signage standards, a photography and story library, print and digital production at pooled rates, and a single visitor and monitoring data format. Wrapped around it, a coaching retainer park and conservancy staff book against, and a shared trade-marketing calendar so 15 areas appear at WTM Africa and Indaba as one delegation rather than fifteen absences. Critically, it is delivered through existing associations rather than as a new CI unit: the studio supplies what NRT, NACSO and MMWCA do not currently provide, which is brand and marketing capability. This is CI's stated 'simple version', the grant-funded technical assistance retainer, built so it does not duplicate the aggregation layer already on the ground.
options.payer: CI and Keystone donors underwrite the first phase. Conservancy associations and park authorities then pay a subscription scaled to size, with production recovered per unit. Lodges and operators in the areas buy studio time at commercial rates, cross-subsidising the parks.
options.governance: No new legal entity in phase one. The studio is hosted inside an existing association or as a CI-managed facility, with a user council of park authorities and associations setting the annual work programme and priorities. The design system itself, rather than a committee, enforces consistency; Harpers Ferry Center holds 400+ park units to one standard through the Unigrid grid rather than through approvals.
anchorBenchmarks: NPS Harpers Ferry Center and Unigrid: 100+ staff, one modular grid for 400+ park units, 24 to 28 million brochures printed a year at a few cents a copy

NACSO: links the support organisations serving Namibia's 86 registered communal conservancies across about 166,000 km2 and 245,000 people, all on one Event Book monitoring system, with one annual State of Community Conservation report; 42 joint-venture lodges operating and N$75m of resident cash income in 2022, 64% of it from joint-venture tourism
MMWCA: 24 conservancies, about 178,700 ha, some 16,500 landowners, 50 tourism partners and a team of 30+; CI already co-created the US$5m Maasai Mara Rescue Fund with MMWCA in 2020

Northern Rangelands Trust: member-owned by 43 community conservancies, pooling governance, security, fundraising and enterprise support; site identities such as Il Ngwesi and Westgate survive intact under it

The Long Run: 60 to 70+ members safeguarding 23m+ acres, Fellow Members given about five years of onsite and remote coaching to reach the GER standard; African members include Grootbos, Tswalu and Sasaab
options.sustainabilityLogic: Marginal cost falls as volume rises: the Harpers Ferry economics only work because one system serves 400+ units. The route off grant is a three-step migration, from donor-funded build, to subscription for the toolkit and data spine, to fee-for-service studio time sold to lodges, operators and associations at commercial rates. Because it rides on associations that already exist, it avoids the secretariat overhead that sank comparable stand-alone bodies.
options.keyRisk: Not one shared-service benchmark in the scan rates high on self-funding. NRT, NACSO and Harpers Ferry Center all rate L. The honest risk is that this option is permanently grant-dependent and simply moves CI's cost from fifteen small bills to one large one. It also does nothing about demand: a park with an excellent brand kit and no distribution is still invisible. The deep-dives must establish what associations actually spend per conservancy and whether any of them would pay a subscription.

options.name: The Keystone Mark
options.archetype: Archetype 2, Site standard, combined with Archetype 3, Enterprise mark
options.oneLine: A tiered Keystone standard that certifies areas against published criteria and licenses a mark to the businesses and products around them, run through national operators in each country, with sites and certified businesses paying the assessment and licence fees.
options.offer: A bronze-to-platinum pathway so areas of uneven capacity can all enter and then climb, rather than 15 areas failing one bar. Certification brings a mark with real consequences, periodic revalidation, a peer network, a shared criteria manual, training and co-operative marketing. A companion enterprise mark extends to lodges, operators and park-edge producers, giving communities a market-access route that carries the park's story. Where credible national schemes already exist, the model recognises them rather than replacing them, which is how Fair Trade Tourism crossed borders cheaply. This is the middle of CI's spectrum: brand credibility and a quality floor without standing up a consumer-facing company.
options.payer: Protected areas and their authorities pay assessment and revalidation fees; certified businesses pay annual licence fees. National operators are funded locally, typically an environmental NGO with a line from a government department, which is how Blue Flag reaches 52 countries. Donors fund standard-setting and the first revalidation cycles.
options.governance: An independent standard owner with a council that issues and withdraws the mark, national operators and juries implementing it country by country, and an accredited third-party assessor. Mutual-recognition agreements with existing national schemes. Renewal on a fixed cycle so the mark stays honest; Geoparks use green, yellow and red cards on a four-year revalidation, Blue Flag re-awards annually.
anchorBenchmarks: Blue Flag (FEE, since 1987): 4,302 beaches, 736 marinas and 158 boats across 52 countries in 2025, against 33 criteria for beaches, run by a national operator in each country; in Morocco through the Mohammed VI Foundation, in Ireland through An Taisce with government funding

UNESCO Global Geoparks: 229 geoparks in 48 countries as at May 2026, revalidated by two evaluators every four years on a green, yellow, red card system, with recent advice to geoparks on visibility, signage and geotourism products mirroring CI's own diagnosis

Slovenia Green: 200+ members including 59 destinations by 2022 on a bronze-to-platinum ladder with three-year renewal, owned by the Slovenian Tourist Board, assessed by GoodPlace against ETIS and GSTC criteria; four municipalities in Karst and Brkini merged into a single destination label on renewal

Fair Trade Tourism: 188 businesses in eight countries, its own certification in South Africa, Madagascar and Mozambique plus mutual recognition of national schemes in Botswana, Kenya, Namibia, Seychelles and Tanzania; certifying a package cost around EUR 3,000, with larger firms subsidising smaller

EUROPARC Charter (ECST): the nearest template for multi-stakeholder brand management at park level, with 1,500+ business partners and 41 tour operators, but down from 164 areas in 20 countries in 2017 to 91 areas in 13 countries on the 2026 factsheet

Certified Wildlife Friendly (WFEN, founded 2007): certified enterprises help conserve 14m+ ha and benefit 500,000+ people as at 2024, including Elephant Pepper in Zambia, showing how a conservation mark travels onto products
options.sustainabilityLogic: Fee income recurs by design because the mark expires. Annual or multi-year renewal converts certification into a subscription, and the enterprise licence widens the fee base from park authorities, who have no money, to lodges, operators and producers, who do. Delivery through nationally funded operators pushes the running cost off CI's balance sheet and onto bodies that already carry it in their own countries.
options.keyRisk: Standards cost more to run than they earn, and the scan contains two warnings. The ECST network contracted from 164 areas to 91. Fair Trade Tourism scaled across eight countries on Swiss SECO funding and now works through a partnership with SATSA, having planned as early as 2012 to outsource certification altogether. The deeper risk is that a mark confers credibility but not demand: it tells a visitor the park is good, it does not tell them the park exists. For 15 emerging areas with low awareness, that may be solving the second problem before the first.

options.name: The Co-Brand Hub
options.archetype: Archetype 4, Place marketer (thematic-route and co-brand hub sub-types). This is the fourth option EY has added beyond the three the benchmark scan proposed.
options.oneLine: A shared storytelling platform that organises the emerging areas into a handful of thematic routes and hands national tourism boards and operators ready-made, co-brandable product and proof for their own campaigns, paid for by those boards, regional bodies and development finance rather than by the parks themselves.
options.offer: Three or four thematic routes that let small, unknown areas borrow appeal from a shared story instead of each building a brand from nothing. An open brand hub of co-brandable assets, trade-ready content and itineraries operators can lift directly, a press and trade programme, and a pipeline of bankable investment opportunities for lodge and airline investors. Deliberately no separate consumer-facing identity competing with Visit Rwanda or its equivalents: the model supplies product and proof into the boards' existing media spend. This is the archetype that answers CI's requirement to reconcile with national destination brands, treating them as the distribution channel rather than as a stakeholder to be managed.
options.payer: National tourism boards and regional bodies of the SADC or KAZA type, using budgets they already spend. Development finance for the build, following the KAZA precedent. CI seeds the platform. Operators pay tiered fees for trade-show presence and magazine or hub placement, as members of Africa's Eden Tourism already do.
options.governance: Hosted under an existing regional body rather than a new secretariat, with a steering committee per route bringing together site managers and national tourism institutions, which is how World Heritage Journeys was run. Boards retain ownership of the national story; the hub owns only the route narrative and the asset library. Where a cross-border legal vehicle is unavoidable, Alpine Pearls' EGTC is the precedent for what one makes possible.
anchorBenchmarks: World Heritage Journeys of the European Union: one storytelling platform for 34 World Heritage sites in 19 countries organised into four thematic routes, published in English, Chinese and French, reporting 1m+ digital impressions a year, with Solimar International leading destination development

KAZA 'Rivers of Life': a co-brand launched across five countries covering around 520,000 km2 and some 228,000 elephants, with an online brand hub built so operators co-brand rather than compete, funded through a KfW Phase III grant and a EUR 5m EU commitment in 2025; the KAZA UniVisa, US$50 for 30 days, shows access policy can matter as much as communication

Signature Experiences of Australia: Tourism Australia packages eight industry-led collectives, among them Luxury Lodges of Australia at about 18 to 19 members, all sold under 'There's Nothing Like Australia' - a collective close in scale to CI's 15 areas, reconciled with a national brand
Slovenia Green: board ownership of the label removes brand rivalry outright

Boundless Southern Africa: the cautionary case, with a secretariat since 2007 and a brand since May 2008 covering SADC's 12 formally recognised TFCAs and a pipeline of 51 bankable investment opportunities, but no published measure of recognition, trade adoption or bookings in 18 years

Visit Rwanda: about GBP 10m a year to Arsenal and more than GBP 80m over eight years; any park brand in Rwanda sits beneath this, not beside it, and the February 2026 DRC appeal to the clubs shows the political exposure that comes with it
options.sustainabilityLogic: The cheapest option per park, because it spends other people's marketing budgets rather than building its own audience. Financial sustainability comes from becoming indispensable to the boards: once a national campaign depends on the hub for its protected-area content, the hub's cost sits inside a recurring public budget line rather than a grant. Operator fees for trade presence provide a second, smaller stream on the Africa's Eden model.
options.keyRisk: This is the archetype with the worst durability record in the whole scan, and CI should weigh that. Boundless Southern Africa has run for 18 years with no published outcome data. Alpine Pearls fell from about 24 villages in six countries to 18 in four. The Commission narrowed EDEN to a single annual winner after its 2019 evaluation, having rewarded 175 destinations in 27 countries. Every place marketer rates L or M on self-funding. The risk is a well-made brochure that nobody adopts, and the test of this option is whether any tourism board will put its own money in.

options.name: The Keystone Collection
options.archetype: Archetype 5, Curator and distributor (hosted or borrowed-brand collection first, independent consortium later)
options.oneLine: A curated collection of lodges, camps and experiences in and around the emerging areas, sold through an existing platform's distribution, loyalty and GDS infrastructure under a hosting agreement, paid for by the member businesses through fees and commissions, with a licence fee flowing back to the parks.
options.offer: Admission on merit against conservation, community and experience criteria that CI controls. Members buy what they cannot build alone: a recognised mark, trade sales, reservations, a shared GDS chain code, an existing loyalty programme and quality assurance. CI takes a licence or royalty back to the protected areas. The design move is deliberate: host the collection on an existing platform first, learn the economics, and only build an independent consortium once membership and margin justify carrying distribution costs. This is CI's stated 'complex version', the Leading Hotels of the World analogue, approached in the order that de-risks it.
options.payer: Member lodges and operators, through membership fees and booking commissions paid to the host platform. A park licence or royalty flows back to the protected areas. CI funds curation, criteria-setting and the first admission rounds for a defined and declared period, then withdraws.
options.governance: A hosting agreement with an established platform, with a CI-chaired admissions and standards committee retaining control of who enters and of the conservation criteria, so the conservation purpose is not diluted by commercial growth targets. Time-limited admission with periodic reassessment. An explicit step-in and exit clause defining the terms on which the collection could be taken independent.
anchorBenchmarks: Beyond Green (Preferred Hotel Group): launched with 24 founding members in 15 countries, a third of them African safari camps and lodges, including &Beyond Bateleur in Kenya, Mnemba in Tanzania, Sossusvlei in Namibia, Wilderness Mombo, DumaTau, Hoanib and Linkwasha, and Xigera; members vetted on 50+ indicators and buying Preferred's distribution technology, shared GDS chain code and I Prefer loyalty programme

Small Luxury Hotels of the World: the Considerate Collection launched in 2021 with 25 hotels and reached 82 in 41 countries by late 2025 inside a portfolio of about 600, with loyalty rented rather than built through a World of Hyatt alliance - the two moves CI could copy, themed sub-collections and borrowed distribution

National Geographic Unique Lodges of the World: launched January 2015 with 24 charter lodges, five of them African (Grootbos, Sabi Sabi Earth Lodge, Rubondo Island Camp, Sayari Camp, Kasbah du Toubkal), reaching 63 properties by around 2020, sold through Virtuoso advisers - proof that borrowing a trusted conservation brand is faster than building one

The Leading Hotels of the World: 400+ independently owned hotels in 80+ countries since 1928, entry by member nomination and inspection; its paid consumer Leaders Club tier (US$150 to US$175 a year) was made free in June 2021, which is where the value sits and where it does not

Relais & Chateaux: a non-profit association running a premium commercial brand at scale, 580 properties in 65 countries, members reporting EUR 3.308bn of business in 2025 and applications up 14% to 615, with African members including Royal Chundu in Zambia and Zarafa Camp and Sitatunga Private Island in Botswana
options.sustainabilityLogic: The only archetype in the scan that consistently rates high on self-funding. LHW has run since 1928 and Relais & Chateaux since 1954 because independent members buy distribution and demand, not goodwill. Hosting rather than building removes the largest fixed cost, so the collection can reach break-even at 20 to 30 members instead of the several hundred an independent consortium needs. The park royalty converts commercial success directly into protected-area revenue, which is CI's actual objective.
options.keyRisk: The commercial collections have already taken Africa's marquee lodges, and the gap is precisely the areas that cannot clear their bar. Every curator benchmark rates L on low-capacity fit. Emerging areas have thin, low-occupancy, sometimes non-existent tourism supply, so the collection may have too little to sell to be worth a platform's time. Member fee structures for LHW, SLH, Beyond Green and National Geographic are all unpublished, which means the economics of CI's preferred complex version are currently unknown. Whether Preferred Hotel Group or SLH would host a Keystone collection, and on what terms, is the single highest-value question in the whole deep-dive programme.

revenueModules: Multi-park visitor pass ('Keystone Pass'). The SANParks Wild Card pools 80+ parks and reserves across five conservation agencies - SANParks, CapeNature, Ezemvelo KZN Wildlife, Msinsi and Big Game Parks in Eswatini - at recent All Parks rates of R835 individual, R1,375 couple and R1,680 family, with international rates from R3,780 and tariffs rising annually with CPI. A tour operator version loads entry vouchers onto guides' cards. It is the best African proof of CI's 'wild card' idea, and it works because five agencies pooled scale around a large domestic market. Open questions: how revenue splits across the five partners, and whether it travels to countries with small domestic markets.

Match facility. Brand USA unlocks a 1:1 match from the ESTA visitor fee against industry cash and in-kind contributions from 800+ partner organisations, capped at US$100m a year and up to US$200m in total, with no general taxpayer money. In-kind media, rooms and flights count towards the match, which crowds in contributions that are not cash. Keystone already uses match logic: the Rob Walton Foundation will match GEF-9 resources directed to Keystone areas with up to US$50m. The caution is equally clear: COVID cut ESTA receipts to US$62m in FY2020, emergency funding was needed in 2022, and 2025 legislation cut the match cap to US$20m.

Imagery or brand licence. The Lion's Share Fund asks brands to pledge 0.5% of media spend on any advertisement featuring an animal. UNDP-led and founded with FINCH, with Mars as founding partner alongside Clemenger BBDO and Nielsen, about 50 brands including Gucci had signed by 2020 against a target of US$100m a year. It monetises wildlife imagery that brands already use without paying for. For CI, a park-brand licence or imagery levy is testable with airlines, banks and beverage brands that trade on African wildlife.

Consumer membership tier. The National Trust earned GBP 309.4m of membership income in 2024/25 from 2.61m memberships covering 5.35m people, against total income of GBP 766.2m and 25.9m visits, with 83.3% retention, 403,000 new members and a GBP 48 young persons' tier that lifted joiners aged 18 to 25 by 39%. It is the reference case for one brand, many places and recurring consumer revenue. But memberships still slipped 0.4% as cost-pressed visitors paid on the day, and LHW abandoned its paid Leaders Club tier in June 2021. Second-phase revenue, once enough parks and a regional customer base exist.

Product and merchandise mark. Certified Wildlife Friendly, run by WFEN since 2007, certifies enterprises and products across agriculture, fibre, food, cosmetics, coffee and tourism; certified enterprises help conserve 14m+ ha and benefit 500,000+ people as at 2024, with African examples including Elephant Pepper in Zambia. Fair Trade Tourism reached 188 businesses in eight countries, largely through mutual recognition of national schemes rather than its own certification. Together they show how a conservation mark travels onto goods, giving communities around a park a merchandise and market-access route that carries the park's story - and maps directly to CI's named merchandise stream.

Member fees and commissions. Africa's Eden Tourism is the only African cross-border identity in the scan that the private sector pays for, on a tiered pay-to-play membership across eight countries, funding roadshows, regional exhibitions and a magazine distributed in 10,000 printed copies through shows, member properties and airlines. Relais & Chateaux's 580 members reported EUR 3.308bn of business in 2025 with applications up 14% to 615. Fee levels for LHW, SLH, Beyond Green, National Geographic Unique Lodges and The Long Run are all unpublished, which makes them a priority deep-dive question rather than a modelling assumption.

Enterprise lending and guest levies. Rewilding Europe Capital had lent more than EUR 1.3m to 20 enterprises by the end of 2018 and deploys EUR 6m from the EIB's Natural Capital Financing Facility; in Portugal's Coa Valley a cluster of loan-backed businesses passes guest levies back to rewilding and land purchase. It monetises through the enterprises around a protected area rather than through the brand itself, which suits areas whose brand has no audience yet. Critics call this the commodification of nature, a stakeholder risk CI should anticipate and address in the design rather than after it.
evaluationFrame: Section 4 of our benchmark scan already rates all 31 benchmarks against nine criteria, and that matrix becomes the scoring frame for the models, so the evidence carries straight through from Activity One into Activity Two. Six criteria come directly from CI's own terms of reference: financial sustainability, aggregation and cost efficiency, conservation-led and culturally appropriate delivery, support for data collection, multi-segment stratification and destination appeal, and fit with national destination brands. Two come from Activity Two's stated conditions: operating across jurisdictions, and working for protected areas of widely varying capacity. The ninth is African evidence, because a model with no African precedent carries more delivery risk. Each model is scored high, medium or low against published evidence rather than preference, and the scoring is shown so CI can dispute it. The weighting is CI's to set, not ours.
